newsitem.title: UK: Rise in U.S. CPI seen providing support for dollar.
newsitem.headline: Rise in U.S. CPI seen providing support for dollar.

text.p: The dollar weathered a higher than expected rise in U.S. inflation data on Wednesday, and growing speculation of a near-term rise in U.S. interest rates will give it further support, currency analysts said.
Market speculation of a rate rise at the policy setting Federal Open Market Committee on March 25 has been simmering for some time and is partly responsible for the dollar's underlying strength.
Wednesday's U.S. CPI figures, which were slightly firmer than expected, were keenly watched in the currency markets as they were the last batch of inflationary data before next week's FOMC meeting.
However, currency analysts were still cautious of the importance of the CPI data in providing clues to likely monetary policy action the Federal Reserve will take.

"It is an important figure with the market on a knife-edge in the run-up to the FOMC, but you could say it's the wrong figure at the right time," said Francis Breedon, foreign exchange economist at Lehman Brothers in London.
Analysts were mindful that Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan has indicated that other factors, such as labour market conditions, were more important to Fed monetary policy.

February headline CPI rose 0.3 percent, above an average forecast of 0.2 percent, while the core figure ex-food and energy was up 0.2 percent as expected. Year-on-year inflation came in at 3.0 percent.
In afternoon Europe, the dollar against the mark was trading at 1.6813, above its late Tuesday level in Europe of 1.6731 marks.
While the CPI increase hardened the view of an imminent rate rise, analysts said that on its own it did not present much of a case for tightening monetary policy.
So far, there have been few indications of any significant inflationary pressures in the U.S. and labour costs remained subdued.
But currency markets were wary of the risk of a pre-emptive strike by the Fed to curb the risk of potential inflation.

"The basic problem is the market's fear of a pre-emptive move by the Fed which means the market can't relax," said Tony Norfield, treasury economist at ABN-Amro in London. "We have to see data biased in a softening direction to ease the sense of a Fed policy move."

The long-running positive growth, low inflation scenario being played out in the U.S. is also increasing nervousness for those convinced such a situation has to end at some point. And a rate hike next week would go a long way to alleviate those concerns and bolster the credibility of the Fed, said analysts.
Bond markets were weaker following the CPI data, initially taking dollar/mark down with it, but analysts saw this dollar reaction as short-lived.
"In the end it has to be good for the dollar. A drop in assets, putting 30-year bond yields above 7.00 percent, has to be positive for the dollar," said ABN-Amro's Norfield.
And if rates are kept steady next week, this will not necessarily be negative for the dollar either because it will keep rate hike sentiment on the boil, maintaining one of the dollar's key props.

"Part of the dollar's strength is in expectation of higher U.S. rates," said Jeremy Stretch, currency strategist at NatWest Bank in London. "If a rate rise doesn't materialise, the economic situation is still positive in the U.S. and positive for the dollar."
